source: Richardson, Kearns, Moss, Wang-Mascianica & Koralus (2026) Theory-grounded evaluation of human-like fallacy patterns in LLM reasoning (ICLR 2026)
finding: Large LLM test with disjunction-type fallacies of the illusory-inference family. 38 models, 383 generated problems chosen so the theory predicts a fallacy. Models were correct on only a minority of these items. Stronger models did not get more items right, but a larger share of their wrong answers were the predicted human fallacy. Reversing premise order blocked the fallacy for many models.
numbers: 383 problems, 38 models (Mistral 7B to GPT-4.5 and Claude 3.7), up to 3,000 output tokens, reasoning models 2,400 thinking tokens. Logically correct: mean 40.6%, min 16.7%, median 31.0%, max 91.7%. Correctness vs Chatbot Arena Elo: r=0.004, p=.981. Share of wrong answers that are the predicted fallacy vs Elo: Spearman 0.360, p=.0265. Fallacies blocked by reversing premises: chatgpt-4o-latest 46.15% (p=.0012), gpt-4.5-preview 68.00% (p=.0024), gemini-2.5-flash-preview 37.27% (p=.0004), deepseek-chat-v3-0324 38.78% (p=.023). Human reference in the paper: about 60% endorsed 'Mary has an ace' (second-hand from Mascarenhas & Koralus).
quote: a larger share of a model's incorrect answers are ETR-predicted fallacies
limits: Erotetic-theory fallacies, not Johnson-Laird illusions as such. Items were built so the fallacy is the theory's output, so there are no matched controls and no human rates on these 383 items. Open-ended 'what follows' format; GPT-4.1-mini translated answers into formal form. Chatbot Arena Elo is a rough capability proxy. Correlational. No frontier late-2026 models, no confidence or self-consistency measure. Authors are the theory authors.
agent_relevance: LLMs do fall for the same kind of disjunction fallacy, and capability does not remove it. This is the closest evidence that an enumeration operator is worth testing (G1). It does not give a human-rate comparison or a confidence signal.

source: Koralus & Wang-Mascianica (2023) Humans in humans out: on GPT converging toward common sense in both success and failure
finding: 61 inference and judgment problems (ETR61), including illusory inferences, given to GPT-3, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 (March 2023). Fallacy production rose with newer models. A small second study tested a prose 'list the questions first' prompt against a plain control prompt.
numbers: Production of ETR-predicted fallacies: GPT-3 18%, GPT-3.5 33%, GPT-4 34%. Any ETR-predicted output: 59%, 77%, 75%. Study 2, fallacies blocked, control prompt vs ETR prompt: GPT-3 4/8 vs 4/8; GPT-3.5 4/17 vs 14/17 (p=.0045); GPT-4 8/19 vs 7/19 (p=.77).
limits: Authors are the theory authors. Items come from the authors' book, mixed task types, only 61 items, tiny cells in study 2, 2023 models. Study 2 used only items where the model had already erred.
agent_relevance: For GPT-4 a plain control prompt blocked as many fallacies as the theory-based prose prompt (8/19 vs 7/19). Prose instructions alone are a weak lever, as in humans (K03). Supports testing a code-built table against a prose warning, not a prose warning alone.

source: Goldvarg & Johnson-Laird (2000) Illusions in modal reasoning, Experiment 1 (Memory & Cognition 28, 282-294)
finding: Reasoning about what is possible. With 'only one premise is true' rubrics, people said an ace was possible when the other premises made it impossible. Controls were easy. Confidence was equally high.
numbers: Exp 1: N=20 Princeton undergraduates, 8 illusory and 8 control problems. Correct on controls 91%, on illusions 15%. All 20 more accurate on controls. Illusions of possibility were more compelling than illusions of impossibility (interaction Wilcoxon Z=2.75, p<.006). Only 3% 'cannot be deduced' answers. Confidence high for all problems.
limits: One lab, authors wrote theory and items, 5-point confidence scale, student sample, no paper allowed, one content type (card hands).
agent_relevance: Re-opens the original for the human illusion rate on modal items: 15% correct vs 91% on controls. That is the human baseline an LLM test must be compared with.

source: Goldvarg & Johnson-Laird (2000) Illusions in modal reasoning, Experiments 2 and 3
finding: Exp 2 repeated the illusions. Exp 3 gave half the participants a check instruction after the first half: check that one premise is still true and the other still false. The check helped a lot on illusions but did not remove them.
numbers: Exp 2: N=20; controls 79% correct, illusions 22%; 19 of 20 better on controls. Exp 3: N=20 in two groups; overall controls 95%, illusions 39%. First half the groups did not differ (help 60%, no help 63%). Second half, illusion problems: help group 71%, no-help group 30% (Mann-Whitney U=10, p<.002). Table 6, illusions of possibility, help group: 0% first half, 57% second half; illusions of impossibility 70% to 85%. Controls with help: 93% and 100% then 90% and 87%. Confidence 4.17 on illusions vs 4.24 on controls.
limits: Tiny groups (about 10 each). The 57% that Yang & Johnson-Laird quoted is one table cell (possibility illusions after the check), not the overall rate (71%). The check was given only after half the problems.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 9 for b11: 57% is a real number in the original but a partial cell. Overall post-check illusion accuracy was 71%, still far from perfect. A check instruction is a partial fix at best.

source: Yang & Johnson-Laird (2000) How to eliminate illusions in quantified reasoning (Memory & Cognition 28, 1050-1059)
finding: Two experiments. Telling people to work out both cases (premise 1 true and 2 false, then premise 2 true and 1 false) closed the gap between illusions and controls, but at a cost on controls.
numbers: Exp 1: N=20. Without instructions: controls 93%, illusions 33%. One-case remedial instruction: illusions 33% to 65%, controls 93% to 79% (z=2.31, p<.01). Overall 63% to 72%. Exp 2: N=20. Without instructions: controls 87%, illusions 39%. Two-case instruction: illusions 39% to 71%, controls 87% to 72% (z=1.99, p<.05). After the instruction no reliable gap between illusions and controls (z=0.44). Overall 63% to 71%.
limits: Students, quantified (not propositional) problems, one lab, small N, indicative and deontic versions mixed. Gain is bounded near 71%, so errors remain on about 29% of items.
agent_relevance: Confirms the human cost figures behind gap 2: a two-case procedure fixes illusions at the price of about 15 points on controls. A code-built table that always fires should be tested for the same cost, and gated if it has it.

source: Santamaria & Johnson-Laird (2000) An antidote to illusory inferences (Thinking & Reasoning 6, 313-333)
finding: Illusions about disjunctions of disjunctions. They shrink strongly when the disjunction is about physical objects (which newspaper ads exist) rather than about the truth of assertions.
numbers: Exp 1: N=32. Controls 98% correct, illusions 16%. Physical disjunctions 61% vs logical 53%. 31% 'yes' with logical vs 19% with physical, the rest 'cannot tell'. Exp 2: N=32, controls 97%, illusions 30%. Exp 3: N=32, controls 100%, illusions 52%, physical 92% vs logical 59%. Discussion summary: illusion accuracy rose from 19% (logical) to 84% (physical) once all premises named the entities explicitly.
limits: Santamaria is a collaborator of Johnson-Laird, student samples. The antidote is a change of content and framing, not a general reasoning fix.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition for gap 4: the size of the illusion depends heavily on framing. Rewriting a task so it names concrete entities is a cheap lever to test next to the table.

source: Khemlani & Johnson-Laird (2009) Disjunctive illusory inferences and how to eliminate them (Memory & Cognition 37, 615-623)
finding: Embedded disjunctions (A or else (B or else C)). Illusions were large. Remedial instruction helped. With a yes/no response format the illusions were much smaller.
numbers: Exp 1: N=18. Exp 2 overall: controls 95% correct, illusions 19% (Wilcoxon z=8.42). Second block, gap between controls and illusions: 34 points for the instructed group vs 79 points for the uninstructed group (Mann-Whitney z=1.71, p<.05); illusion accuracy differed between groups in block 2 (z=2.44, p<.01). Confidence 5.45 to 6.26 of 7. Exp 3: controls 81%, illusions 63% (z=3.03). Extra inference 65% vs 61% (n.s.); property problems 69% vs relation problems 57%.
limits: This is the 2009 journal text, so it settles what the paper says for Exp 2 and 3. The 2008 proceedings version was not compared line by line, so the a08/b06/b07 conflict is resolved only toward the 2009 numbers. Exp 3 used yes/no (chance 50%).
agent_relevance: Response format changes the illusion size a lot (19% correct vs 63% with a yes/no question). An LLM test must fix the answer format and report it, or results will not compare to humans.

source: Espino, Orenes & Moreno-Rios (2024) Illusory inferences in conditional expressions (Memory & Cognition 52, 1687-1699)
finding: A different lab (Spain, Spanish-language items) found the conditional illusion. It also found that 'only if' and 'if and only if' wording changes the illusory answer, as the model theory predicts and a suppositional account does not.
numbers: Exp 1: N=80 UNED undergraduates. 'if-then' problem: 69% said 'ace' (illusory), 24% 'may or may not', 8% correct. 'only if': 64% 'may or may not', 31% 'ace', 5% correct. Controls vs illusions correct: 83% vs 6% (z=7.82, r=.87). Confidence 3.9 vs 4.0 (n.s.). Exp 2: N=79. Exp 3 repeated the pattern: controls 68% vs illusions 30% correct (r=.64). Power analysis aimed at 79 participants (g=.2, power .95).
limits: Authors thank Khemlani and have worked with Johnson-Laird's group before, so only partly independent. Four problems per person (2 illusory, 2 control). Conditional illusions only, not disjunction illusions.
agent_relevance: Best recent human replication with effect sizes and N near 80. The effect is large (r about .87 in Exp 1) and survives translation. Confidence again fails to flag the error. Human anchor for any LLM illusion test.

source: Walsh & Johnson-Laird (2004) Co-reference and reasoning (Memory & Cognition 32, 96-106)
finding: When the same person is named across premises, people reason better about valid disjunctions but also fall for illusions. Co-reference changes which possibilities get built.
numbers: Exp 1: N=30. Exp 3: N=35. Control problems 78% correct, illusory problems only 10% correct; 34 of 35 participants were more accurate on controls. Predicted (illusory) responses were the majority response on illusory problems.
limits: Same network as Johnson-Laird. Wording (who the premises are about) is a strong lever on the error rate, which complicates cross-study comparison. Only the abstract, Exp 3 results and parts of Exp 1 were read closely.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition for gap 4: wording that links premises to one individual changes illusion rates. Item generation for an LLM test should randomise referents.

source: Dames, Klauer & Ragni (2021) The stability of syllogistic reasoning performance over time (Thinking & Reasoning)
finding: Full text read (the earlier pass had only the abstract). 100 German adults did all 64 syllogisms in two sessions one week apart, with no feedback. The gain came inside session 1 and only on valid items. The authors give two explanations, aversion to the 'no valid conclusion' answer, and a new strategy wrongly applied to invalid items. They do not settle between them.
numbers: N=100, 64 production syllogisms (27 valid, 37 invalid), German content. Session 1: overall 50.1%, valid 55.5%, invalid 46.1%. Session 2: overall 52.7%, valid 60.3%, invalid 47.2%. Trial-number slope significant only for valid items in session 1 (p<.001). On valid items a difference of -6.9% for multiple-model vs -0.6% for single-model problems (t=-3.79, p<.001), which the text reads as fewer NVC answers; the extracted line does not label the measure. Fluid intelligence (Raven) predicted larger retest gains on invalid items. No feedback.
limits: Gain on valid items came with fewer NVC answers, which would also lower accuracy on some invalid items, so a bias shift and real learning are not separated. Authors call for more research. A ceiling effect on single-model items could explain part. 53% of participants reported a strategy.
agent_relevance: Gap 7, human side: the gain is at least partly an NVC-rate shift, but not shown to be only that. For an agent, in-context history can move the NVC rate, so score valid and invalid items separately. No LLM test of 'history shifts only the NVC rate' was found.

source: Bell (1999) The model method, unpublished Princeton PhD thesis; reported in Johnson-Laird (2012) Mental models and consistency, and Johnson-Laird (2024) Mistakes in thinking about cognitive science
finding: Two later texts by Johnson-Laird report Bell's 'model method' (list the possibilities, strike out those later premises rule out). The two reports give different numbers. The original is an unpublished thesis. No independent replication was found.
numbers: 2012 chapter: accuracy 65% to 95%, correct responses 25 s to 15 s. 2024 commentary: 95% vs 63% for controls, 15 s vs 24 s, 2 minutes of teaching, also worked without paper. No N, test statistic or design in either text. The 2012 example is a five-statement 'hovering' problem solved by listing three possibilities and then two.
limits: Same author twice, numbers drift between 2012 and 2024 (65 vs 63, 25 vs 24 s). Thesis not found online. Both reports are by the theory's author.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 stays open. Treat 95% vs 63% as an unverified anecdote. The method (list possibilities, delete those the next premise rules out) is what a code-built table does, so only an own test will tell.

source: Eisape, Tessler, Dasgupta, Sha, Steenkiste & Linzen (2024) A systematic comparison of syllogistic reasoning in humans and language models (NAACL)
finding: Re-read for gap 5. PaLM 2 models on all 64 syllogisms. Scale helps on average but not consistently. Models almost never answer 'nothing follows' with zero-shot chain of thought.
numbers: Best model accuracy about 75% on the 27 syllogisms with a conclusion; the two largest models beat human accuracy, but the largest is below the second largest. 'Nothing follows' (correct for 37 syllogisms) accuracy close to 0% for the models; humans are also reluctant but far higher. Models beat humans on some hard multiple-model items, e.g. IE4. Variable-order effects appear in both humans and models. Prompt method matters (appendix B.3 gives a way to elicit NVC).
limits: 2023 models only, no frontier or reasoning models, main analyses on the 27 non-NVC items. No clean accuracy-by-model-count curve for current models. Gap 5 (frontier models, model-count curve, NVC candidate plus search) stays open.
agent_relevance: Do not read a model-count curve for current models from this paper. Test NVC separately from the 27 valid items, with an explicit 'no valid conclusion' option.

source: Bertolazzi, Gatt & Bernardi (2024) A systematic analysis of LLMs as soft reasoners: the case of syllogistic inferences
finding: Re-opened (was not rechecked in the earlier pass). Open pretrained models fail on invalid syllogisms and show content effects on valid ones. Fine-tuning fixes both; in-context examples do not teach 'nothing follows'.
numbers: Zero-shot CoT, generative task. Humans (Khemlani & Johnson-Laird 2012): 44.63% on valid, 40.97% on invalid. LLaMA-3 8B instruct: valid 78.15% (believable), invalid 30.28%. LLaMA-3 70B: invalid 10.28%; 70B instruct 32.50%. Content effect (valid, unbelievable vs believable): -17.07% for 8B instruct, -8.18% for 70B base, +5.46% (not significant) for 70B instruct. Contradictory answers: LLaMA-3 8B 1.09%, Pythia 18.91%. SFT near ceiling on both validities.
limits: Open-weight models up to 70B, 2024, base and instruct. No frontier or reasoning models. Fine-tuning is out of scope for a scaffold-only agent.
agent_relevance: Content effect is real for 2024 open models and mostly absent for the largest instruction-tuned one. Whether frontier models keep it is addressed only by d14. Gap 8 partly closed, gap 5 still open.

source: Poddar, Sahoo & Ghosh (2025) Understanding syllogistic reasoning in LLMs from formal and natural language perspectives
finding: 14 recent models (Gemini 2.5, GPT-OSS-20B, GLM-4.6, Kimi-K2, Qwen3, Llama 3 series, Gemma 3) on 160 syllogisms with validity and believability crossed. Strong models were near perfect on validity and showed almost no belief bias. Weaker ones showed large belief bias. On the plausibility question some strong models were near chance.
numbers: 160 items (76 valid, 84 invalid; 82 congruent, 78 incongruent). Four prompt types, three temperatures; McNemar analysis N=6,720 evaluations. Belief bias (congruent minus incongruent accuracy): mean +10.81 pp, p=.0280, d=0.66; 12 of 14 models positive; top-tier models under 2 pp; worst +46.9 pp. Correlation between ability and bias -0.565. Natural-language plausibility accuracy about 52% for one model.
limits: Task is to judge valid or invalid, not to generate a conclusion, so there is no 'nothing follows' production and no model-count analysis. Table cells were garbled in text extraction, so I rely on captions and prose. Only 23.8% of items have believable conclusions.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 for 2025 models: belief bias nearly vanishes for the best models on a judge-validity task but not for mid-tier ones. A counterexample step should be tested on mid-tier models where it can matter, and gated off for strong ones.

source: Zang et al. (2026) A syllogistic probe: tracing the evolution of logic reasoning in large language models
finding: Syllogism scoring depends on whether traditional logic (existential import) or modern logic is assumed. Larger and 'thinking' models move toward modern logic. Only the abstract and introduction were read in detail.
numbers: Abstract claims: (i) model size scaling promotes the shift toward modern logic; (ii) thinking is an efficient accelerator beyond parameter scaling; (iii) the base model decides how easily the shift happens. The introduction cites GPT-5 and Gemini-3-Pro-Preview as motivation; which models were tested and per-model numbers were not extracted.
limits: No numbers extracted. Existential import is an item-labelling problem for the 64 syllogisms: a conclusion such as 'some A are C' from all-premises is valid under one logic and not the other.
agent_relevance: For any 64-syllogism test, fix and state the existential-import convention in the grader, or reasoning models may be scored wrong for being more modern-logical than the answer key.

source: Mondorf & Plank (2024) Comparing inferential strategies of humans and large language models in deductive reasoning (ACL)
finding: Propositional problems (conditionals, disjunctions) with Llama 2, Mistral and Zephyr. Models show supposition following and chain construction like humans, but a correct final answer often rests on unsound steps.
numbers: Llama-2-70B reasoned soundly in about 31.7% of cases; Zephyr-7B and Mistral-7B-Instruct lower; Llama-2-7B showed no sound reasoning. Model size correlated with strategy use (r(298)=0.45). The symbolic (truth-table) strategy was rare.
limits: Open 2023-24 models, small problem set, hand-annotated strategies. Not an illusion test.
agent_relevance: Spontaneous enumeration of all possibilities is rare in LLMs, so an enumeration operator adds a behaviour the model does not show on its own. That it helps is still unsupported.

source: Holliday, Mandelkern & Zhang (2024) Conditional and modal reasoning in large language models (EMNLP)
finding: 25 LLMs on conditional and epistemic modal inference patterns. All except the GPT-4 family made basic mistakes with conditionals. Even GPT-4 gave logically inconsistent modal judgments. Zero-shot chain of thought helped. Answers to hard conditional inferences often did not match reported human judgments.
numbers: 25 LLMs, temperature 0, zero-shot, few-shot and CoT conditions. GPT-4 family best; Claude 3 Opus and Gemini 1.5 Pro behind. Smaller models near 50% on the simple-logic task (Figure 1).
limits: Philosophy-style patterns (modus tollens, 'might', disjunctive syllogism), not Johnson-Laird illusions. Abstract and results prose read; not every table.
agent_relevance: Supports a weaker claim: modal reasoning ('might', 'possible') is a weak spot even for the best 2024 models, which is where the model theory predicts illusions.

source: Khemlani & Johnson-Laird (2021) Reasoning about properties: a computational theory (Psychological Review), mReasoner simulations
finding: Re-read for gap 6. The search parameter is the probability that the program looks for a counterexample. Best-fitting values differ by reasoner group. The fits are in-sample with free parameters. No test asks what should trigger the search.
numbers: 20 individuals (Johnson-Laird & Steedman 1978): mean best-fit r=.70 (range .57 to .86), worst-fit mean .24; no concordance of parameter settings (Kendall's W=.28, p=.33). Three clusters: poorest reasoners size 2.0, search .4, reconclude .6; best reasoners size 4.5, search .8, reconclude .6; fits r=.78, .83, .91. Grid of 1,512 parameter settings, each of 64 syllogisms simulated 100 times. This sample answered NVC 45% vs 30% elsewhere (z=6.19, p<.001).
limits: Authors' own implementation, four free parameters, fits chosen on the same data. Search is a propensity, not a trigger rule.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 stays open. The search parameter says deliberate search separates good from poor reasoners, not when to fire it. A code-detected signal (sample disagreement, unbelievable answer) is our hypothesis, with no direct test.

source: Khemlani, Lotstein & Johnson-Laird (2012) The probabilities of unique events (PLoS ONE 7: e45975)
finding: Estimates of conjunctions tend to split the difference between the two conjuncts, which violates the joint probability distribution (JPD). Verbal estimates err in the same way.
numbers: Exp 1: N=39 online (Mechanical Turk). JPD violated on 56% of trials. Verbal judgments violated on 34%. Exp 2: N=18; violations on 49% of problems even assuming multiplication was possible; raising P(B) raised violations from 52% to 61% (Wilcoxon z=2.14).
limits: Online samples, the theory's authors, a program fit with free parameters. Not an LLM study.
agent_relevance: Human baseline for gap 10. Counting rows of a full state table in code gives a coherent JPD by construction. Whether LLM errors are the same kind was not tested here.

source: Zhu & Griffiths (2024; v2 2025) Incoherent probability judgments in large language models
finding: Four LLMs (GPT-4, GPT-3.5-turbo, LLaMA-2 7B and 70B) give probability judgments that break probability identities in human-like ways. Repeating the same question gives an inverted-U mean-variance relation, as in humans.
numbers: 24 event pairs; identities for negation, conjunction and disjunction; repeats at temperature 1.0; the Bayesian Sampler fits better than probability-plus-noise (qualitative).
limits: 2023-24 models, direct numeric judgments with no scaffold, no counting-table condition. Explanation by implicit Bayesian inference is the authors' proposal.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 stays open for the fix. LLMs do give incoherent probability judgments, so there is something for a code-counted table to fix. No study tested a counting table or compared it with sum-to-one normalisation.

source: Girotto & Gonzalez (2001) Solving probabilistic and statistical problems: a matter of information structure and question form (as cited in Johnson-Laird et al. 1999)
finding: Original not opened. The 53% vs 8% figure (evidence line a14) remains second-hand. A look for an open full text through OpenAlex returned other papers by these authors but not this one.
numbers: No new numbers. Earlier figure: 53% correct with the counted-chances format vs 8% on a control problem, as cited.
limits: Gap 9 is half closed: the Goldvarg & Johnson-Laird 57% was resolved (d04); the Girotto & Gonzalez 53% vs 8% was not.
agent_relevance: Do not quote 53% vs 8% as established.

source: Bertolazzi, Pezzelle & Bernardi (2026, v3) How language models conflate logical validity with plausibility: a representational analysis of content effects
finding: Ten open models (Qwen-2.5, Qwen-3, Gemma-3) judged validity of syllogisms with plausible and implausible content. Content effects exist in all and are smaller with chain of thought than zero-shot. Validity and plausibility are encoded in nearly the same direction; the more aligned, the bigger the content effect. A steering vector that separates them cut the bias in two models.
numbers: Zero-shot accuracy 80.61% (Qwen3-4B) to 90.91% (Qwen3-32B); zero-shot content effect (CE) 0.063 to 0.418; Gemma-3 accuracy 81.02 to 87.29%, CE 0.129 to 0.213. Chain of thought: CE from -0.006 to 0.147, all models above 89% accuracy, several above 97%. Regression of CE on vector similarity beta=0.557, p=0.017; zero-shot adds 0.188 CE vs chain of thought (p<0.001). Steering: Qwen2.5-32B accuracy 81.62 to 82.21, CE 0.348 to 0.072; Qwen3-14B accuracy 86.54 to 96.70, CE 0.213 to 0.043.
limits: Open models up to 32B only, no frontier API reasoning model. Needs hidden states, so it cannot be a prompt-level scaffold. Plausibility is binary. CE scale is the authors' own and is not the same as the +10.81 point figure in d14.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 half closed. Belief bias is still present in mid-size 2025 models and chain of thought lowers it, which fits d14 (top models under 2 points). It does not test a counterexample step against flag-and-reason. Keep the content-swapped check (G2) but expect small gains on strong models.

source: Wan, Wu, Wang, Zhao, Chen & Li (2025, v4) Derailer-Rerailer: adaptive verification for efficient and reliable language model reasoning
finding: A cheap sampled-agreement check (Derailer) decides which questions get an expensive verification pass (Rerailer). Triggered verification matched or beat always-on verification at a fraction of the tokens on math, symbolic and commonsense tasks. Questions that are stably right or stably wrong are skipped.
numbers: Overall accuracy, tokens in thousands. Claude-3.5-Sonnet: zero-shot CoT 72.7 at 0.108; self-consistency 79.8 at 1.732; Rerailer always on 80.0 at 1.458; Derailer+Rerailer 82.1 at 0.592. Llama-3.1-70B: Rerailer always on 66.3 at 1.652; Derailer+Rerailer 68.1 at 0.648. GPT-4o-mini: Rerailer always on 65.8 at 1.539; Derailer+Rerailer 68.1 at 0.639. Error analysis: Rerailer turns 9.5% of wrong answers right and breaks 1.8% of right ones.
limits: Not logic or illusion items: math, symbolic and commonsense. The trigger is answer disagreement over n samples. It cannot catch a confidently wrong error that is the same in every sample, which is what an illusory inference is (K02, K07). Authors' own comparison, token cost includes the sampling check.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 partly closed for the cheap trigger: disagreement-triggered verification beat always-on at lower tokens on other tasks. Illusion and syllogism errors repeat across samples, so a disagreement trigger will miss them. Add item-structure triggers from code (multiple-model item, 'only one is true' rubric, nothing-follows candidate). Counterexample search as the triggered step is untested.

source: Sable-Meyer & Mascarenhas (2021) Indirect illusory inferences from disjunction: a new bridge between deductive inference and representativeness (Review of Philosophy and Psychology)
finding: An independent lab (Paris) used the Walsh and Johnson-Laird disjunction illusion with premises that do not match in words but are linked by world knowledge (brake depressed, car slowed down). People fell for it at rates close to the classic illusion. How often was predicted by an independent rating of the causal link between the two statements. This contradicts the exact-matching step of mental model theory and of the erotetic theory.
numbers: Norming study: 242 recruited, 238 analysed (Mechanical Turk). Exp 1: 80 recruited, 64 analysed; valid controls accepted 87% (+-2.3), invalid controls 26% (+-3.2); targets differ from chance and both controls (all p<.001); acceptance predicted by link strength, F(1,5)=45.0, p=.001, slope .97 (SE .14), R2=.9. Exp 2: 80 recruited, 70 analysed; valid 90%, invalid 20%; targets p=.0066 vs chance; F(1,5)=6.92, p=.046, slope .69, R2=.58. Text cites about 85% acceptance of the classic fallacy in earlier studies, including Mascarenhas and Koralus 2017.
limits: Mechanical Turk, online, 7 target items per experiment (so 5 df). Tests the matching component, not the whole theory. Authors favour a rival (erotetic) account. Better performance on controls went with a steeper fall for the illusion, so inattention does not explain it. Pragmatics and item order were not manipulated.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 half closed. The illusion replicates in a lab independent of Johnson-Laird, with controls handled correctly. The trigger is wider than word overlap: knowledge links between premises also cause it. Code cannot detect illusion risk from string overlap alone.

source: Ghasemi, Handley & Howarth (2023; preprint 2022) Illusory intuitive inferences: matching heuristics explain logical intuitions (Cognition 105417)
finding: A competing explanation for fast correct logic judgments. Four experiments show the apparent intuitive logic effect follows a surface matching heuristic. It goes with logic when matching points to the logical answer, reverses when matching points the other way, and disappears when matching gives no cue. Accuracy on conflict items fell below chance when matching and logic were misaligned.
numbers: 4 experiments, total N=409 students; 64 arguments per participant, belief vs logic instructions. Exp 2 belief-instruction accuracy .66 non-conflict vs .59 conflict; misaligned items below 50% chance.
limits: About conflict effects under belief instructions, not the Johnson-Laird illusions. Students, online, abstract and pseudo-logical items. I read the abstract, introduction, Experiments 1 and 2; Experiments 3 and 4 only skimmed.
agent_relevance: Supports the caution that a confident wrong answer can come from a surface matching rule rather than a missing model. A possibility table helps only if code builds it from the premises. Item sets where matching and logic disagree are a good diagnostic.

source: He, He, Liang, Zhou, Sun, Yu & Xiao (2025, v2) Order doesn't matter, but reasoning does: training LLMs with order-centric augmentation
finding: Follow-up on premise order. It cites reordering as causing up to a 40% drop (Chen et al. 2024 and another study). It fine-tunes open models of 7B to 70B on logic benchmarks with shuffled premises and gets gains on shuffled tests. No frontier or reasoning model was evaluated.
numbers: Condition-shuffling gains of 7 to 15 points are claimed in the text for fine-tuned LLaMA2-13B, LLaMA3-8B, Mistral-7B and Llama-3.3-70B. I could not tie a baseline premise-order drop to one table cell (layout scrambled).
limits: Training-based, so not usable in a scaffold. Models are small and 2023-24. The over-30% drop is quoted from Chen et al. 2024, not re-measured on current models.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 stays open: no 2025-26 premise-order measurement on frontier or reasoning models was found. Independent premises can be reordered freely and dependent steps cannot, so a code step that sorts premises by dependency is sound in design, but its effect at equal tokens is untested.

source: Tennant et al. (2026) Normative robustness as a frontier for non-verifiable reasoning in LLMs (Google DeepMind)
finding: Four frontier models in 48,000 simulated multi-turn moral deliberations. Models ignored irrelevant distractors, but the order of the premises changed the moral judgment in 13 to 22% of cases, and single-turn vs multi-turn changed it in 10 to 24%.
numbers: 48,000 deliberations, 4 frontier LLMs; order effect 13-22% of cases; duration effect 10-24%; stated user view moves reasoning by up to 6.5% on average.
limits: Moral reasoning, not deduction; no ground truth; order of arguments, not logical premises. Abstract and setup read only.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence that order sensitivity persists in 2026 frontier models, in a different task. Not a deduction number. Gap 10 stays open.

source: Search log, this pass (OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, arXiv, WebSearch, 2026-10-21): frontier and reasoning LLMs on Johnson-Laird illusions, on the 64 syllogisms with a fixed existential-import key, on possibility tables, on counting tables, on premise reordering
finding: No paper found that tests o1/o3/R1-class or current frontier chat models on Johnson-Laird's illusory inferences with matched controls. The only LLM illusion studies stay Koralus and Wang-Masciantica 2023 (GPT-3 to GPT-4) and Richardson et al. 2026 (38 models, disjunction type). Nothing found on an explicit no-valid-conclusion option plus counterexample search on frontier models, a code-built possibility table on illusion items, a code counting table for probability, or code-reordered premises on current models.
numbers: About 15 searches on illusory, mental-model, syllogism and premise-order terms for 2025-26 models gave no direct hit. This is a negative search result, not proof of absence.
limits: Search engines mostly returned older human work and arXiv keyword search was poor. Papers could sit in venues that are not indexed.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1, 2, 4, 9 and 10 need our own experiment; there is no outside number to lean on. Plan them as the first tests in the harness.
